summary: Specifies the conventions for using the U.S. National Security Agency's Suite B algorithms in S/MIME. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 6318.

eli5.summary: Rules for using a set of government-approved secret codes in secure email. It is now outdated.

subtitle: Using NSA-approved cryptography for secure email

tldr.problem: Organizations need to protect email with cryptography that meets government security guidelines, requiring a consistent set of algorithms.
tldr.mechanism: Suite B defines two security levels using elliptic curve signatures, key agreement, AES encryption, and SHA hashing, with detailed conventions for how to apply them in S/MIME.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is historic and replaced by RFC 6318.

facts.label: Level 1 signature algorithm
facts.value: ECDSA with P-256 curve and SHA-256

facts.label: Level 2 signature algorithm
facts.value: ECDSA with P-384 curve and SHA-384

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.content:
RFC 5008 specifies how to use the United States National Security Agency's Suite B algorithms in S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions). S/MIME is the standard way to digitally sign and encrypt email messages. The RFC provides conventions for using Suite B algorithms to secure email, drawing on existing specifications while defining new algorithm identifiers where needed.

Suite B offers two security levels. Security Level 1 uses 128-bit strength algorithms, while Security Level 2 uses 192-bit strength algorithms. The RFC specifies which algorithms go with each level, ensuring that implementations are consistent.
sections.eli5: This tells email programs how to scramble messages using special approved secret codes that come in two strengths, a weaker one and a stronger one.

sections.title: Suite B Algorithms
sections.content:
For signed messages, Suite B uses ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) for signing and SHA for hashing. At Security Level 1, the ECDSA signature uses the P-256 elliptic curve and SHA-256 hashing. At Security Level 2, it uses the P-384 curve and SHA-384 hashing.

For encrypted messages, Suite B uses ECDH (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman) for key agreement to establish a shared secret. The shared secret is then used with a key derivation function to generate a key for AES Key Wrap, which encrypts the content encryption key. The content itself is encrypted with AES-128-CBC at Level 1 or AES-256-CBC at Level 2.
sections.eli5: For signing, it uses a special kind of math (elliptic curves) and a safety check number (hash). For encrypting, it uses the same kind of math to agree on a secret, then AES to scramble the actual message.

sections.title: Message Format and Key Management
sections.content:
Signed S/MIME messages use CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax) structures, with algorithm identifiers specifying which Suite B algorithms apply. The signature covers the message content and is verified using the signer's ECDSA public key from a certificate.

Encrypted messages use ephemeral-static ECDH, meaning the sender generates a temporary key pair and uses the recipient's static key (from a certificate) to agree on a secret. This shared secret is processed through a key derivation function (KDF) based on SHA-256 at Level 1 or SHA-384 at Level 2. The resulting key is used to wrap the content-encryption key, which then encrypts the message.

Each message includes a 16-octet random initialization vector for AES CBC mode. The RFC specifies that the elliptic curve point representing the sender's ephemeral key should normally be in uncompressed form.
sections.eli5: The message includes the sender's temporary key so the receiver can agree on a secret. That secret is then used to lock up the actual message encryption key with AES, and the message itself with AES as well.

sections.title: Certificates and Public Keys
sections.content:
Both ECDSA signature keys and ECDH encryption keys use the same algorithm identifier in certificates, but the key usage field indicates the intended purpose. Implementations should use separate keys for signing and encryption, though using the same key for both is permitted.

The RFC specifies that the namedCurve choice MUST be used in certificates, with the OID for P-256 or P-384 explicitly identifying which curve the key uses. For Suite B, implementations MUST support the uncompressed form of elliptic curve points and MAY support compressed form.
sections.eli5: Email programs need to know which math curve (P-256 or P-384) a person's key uses, so the certificate says it explicitly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that the algorithms themselves have been defined in previous documents, and Suite B just specifies how to use them in S/MIME. Users must choose the appropriate security level for their risk environment; Level 2 provides stronger protection than Level 1.

For both signed and encrypted messages, Suite B provides consistent cryptographic strength across all operations. The security considerations in related RFCs (RFC 3852 for CMS, RFC 3278 for elliptic curve cryptography, and RFC 3565 for AES) apply to Suite B implementations. The effective key space is limited by the size of the shared secret (Z) produced by ECDH, which is 256 bits at Level 1 and 384 bits at Level 2.
sections.eli5: Pick a security level based on how important your email is. All the math recipes are strong, but follow the rules carefully.
